title: Bharata's journey
hookLine: a prince sets out with an army to give a crown away, and at every stop someone thinks he's come to kill
carry: bharata's love comes to give, not take

cards: The ministers gather and do the obvious thing: they offer Bharata the throne. He says no, in front of everyone. The eldest son is king.
I'm going to the forest to bring Rama home, and if he won't come, I'll stay there in his place. Then he sets out, and not quietly. Road builders go ahead clearing a path.
Behind him come the queens, the priest Vasishtha, the citizens and an army. Which, from a distance, looks exactly like what it isn't.

teach.b: Watch the road, because the same scene happens three times. First, the Ganga at Shringaverapura. Guha, the boatman king who ferried Rama across, sees the army and tells his people to guard the river.
Why would Bharata need soldiers, unless he means Rama harm? He meets Bharata with gifts and a careful question. Bharata answers plainly, and Guha believes him.

teach.h: THE GRASS BED UNDER THE TREE.
teach.b: Then Guha shows him the spot under the tree where Rama and Sita slept on a bed of grass, and tells how Lakshmana stood watch all night. Bharata sees the crushed grass and is overwhelmed.
Second, Bharadvaja's hermitage, where Rama stayed too.
The sage welcomes him, then asks outright: you're not here to harm an innocent man, are you? Bharata is hurt, and answers again.
The sage believes him, and by the power of his austerity feeds the whole army a feast fit for the gods. Third, Chitrakoot.
Lakshmana climbs a tall sal tree, sees the dust and the banners of Ayodhya, and wants to fight. Bharata has come to finish us, he says. Rama stops him.
Bharata loves us more than his own life. He hasn't come for that. Three times, the same suspicion.
Twice it takes a conversation to clear it. The third time, Rama doesn't need one.
He already knows his brother. And Hindu tradition never forgot this brother.

teach.h: BHAKTI: LOVE THAT COMES TO GIVE.
teach.b: Tulsidas, who retold the Ramayana in Hindi, gives Bharata's love for Rama some of his most moving pages, and many devotees hold Bharata up as a model of bhakti, devotion: love that comes to give, not to take.
Everyone on that road saw an army. Rama saw a heart that wanted nothing for itself.

how: Ramayana tellers often follow Bharata's road through the same stops Rama made, Guha's river and Bharadvaja's hermitage, so the two journeys mirror each other.

o: his road to the forest to beg Rama to come home
his march to attack Rama and keep the throne
his flight from Ayodhya to escape Kaikeyi's anger

games.q: suspected on the road — tap the pairs.
p: guards the Ganga against the army
asks if he means Rama harm
climbs a sal tree and wants to fight

s: Bharata goes to the forest to take Rama's place if Rama won't return
he tells the assembly the eldest son is king.
he questions Bharata, believes him, and feeds the whole army.
Rama agrees with Lakshmana that Bharata has come to fight
Rama says Bharata loves them more than his own life.

games.q: you're Rama on Chitrakoot. Lakshmana sees Ayodhya's banners and says Bharata has come to finish you. what do you see?
o: an army, so we arm ourselves.
a brother who wants nothing for himself.
a rival we can bargain with.
games.why: Rama stops Lakshmana: Bharata loves us more than his own life. tradition holds Bharata up as bhakti, love that comes to give, not take.

practice: Picture one person you trust without needing proof, the way Rama trusts Bharata, and notice what that trust is built on: years, small kept promises, how they treated you when it cost them something.
Let a little gratitude rise, and stay with it.

wordCard.voice: Bharata's journey. Guha suspects him, Bharadvaja questions him, Lakshmana wants to fight him. Rama alone says: he comes in love.

orig.note: Sanskrit bharata: Rama's brother's name. a different, older King Bharata is the one tradition links to Bhārata, a name for India.

carryVoice: Your line: Bharata's love comes to give, not take. Everyone saw an army; Rama saw his brother's heart. Day five hundred forty-seven, done.
